title: Develop and update networks for extension delivery

lessons.title: Why networks matter in extension
lessons.html:
No extensionist works alone

A single extension officer in a South African district may serve hundreds or even thousands of farmers across a wide area. It is impossible to deliver every service personally. Effective extension depends on a network: a set of relationships with people and organisations that provide knowledge, inputs, finance, markets and support to farmers.

Who belongs in an extension network

GroupExamplesWhat they offer
GovernmentProvincial Department of Agriculture, state veterinarian, animal health technicians, local municipalityProgrammes, disease control, infrastructure, grants
Research and trainingAgricultural Research Council, universities, agricultural collegesNew technology, trials, training
Commodity and farmer bodiesCommodity organisations, study groups, farmer associations, cooperativesTechnical support, mentors, collective action
Private sectorInput suppliers, agribusinesses, banks, buyers, abattoirs, packhousesInputs, credit, markets, technical advice
CommunityTraditional leaders, ward councillors, churches, NGOs, lead farmersAccess, trust, mobilisation

Benefits of a strong network

  • Farmers get faster and more complete answers because you know who to refer them to.
  • Resources are shared, for example a supplier sponsors seed for a demonstration plot.
  • Duplication is reduced when organisations working in the same ward coordinate.
  • You learn about new technology, market prices and risks early.
  • Lead farmers and study groups multiply your reach through farmer-to-farmer learning.

Think of your network as part of your professional capital. It must be built deliberately, maintained regularly and reviewed often, because people change jobs, programmes end and new role players appear.

lessons.title: Building the network: mapping and making contact
lessons.html:
Step by step network development

1. Map stakeholders

Start with the needs of your clients. If a group of smallholder vegetable growers wants to sell to a local supermarket, you need contacts in irrigation, input supply, food safety, packaging, transport and buying. List every organisation and person who could help, then rate each on two questions: how much influence or value they have, and how interested they are in your clients. High value, high interest partners get the most attention.

2. Make contact professionally

  • Introduce yourself, your organisation and your clients clearly and briefly.
  • Explain what you want and also what the partner gains, such as new customers, research sites or meeting their social responsibility goals.
  • Use existing forums: farmers' days, district agricultural forums, commodity meetings, shows and auctions.
  • Follow up in writing after a meeting with a short summary and agreed next steps.

3. Agree on roles

For formal partnerships, write down who will do what, by when, and with what resources. A memorandum of understanding is useful when money, land or equipment is involved. Keep agreements realistic and within your mandate; check with your supervisor before committing your organisation.

4. Record your network

Keep a contact register: name, organisation, role, phone, email, area of expertise, date of last contact and notes. A simple spreadsheet or the contact module of a farm or extension system is enough. Respect privacy: store personal details securely and use them only for the purpose they were given, in line with the Protection of Personal Information Act.

Ethics in networking

Remain neutral. Do not accept gifts or favours that could be seen as influencing which supplier or buyer you recommend to farmers. Present clients with options and let them decide.

lessons.title: Maintaining and updating the network
lessons.html:
Keeping the network alive

Networks decay when they are not used. A contact who has not heard from you in two years may have moved, retired or lost interest. Updating your network is a continuous task.

Regular maintenance

  • Review your contact register at least every quarter. Confirm phone numbers and roles, and remove outdated entries.
  • Share useful information with partners, such as reports from demonstrations or farmer feedback. Networks run on give and take.
  • Invite partners to farmers' days and report-back meetings so they see the value of their contribution.
  • Thank partners publicly when appropriate, for example at a field day.

Evaluating the network

Once a year, ask: Which partners delivered real benefits to farmers? Which relationships are inactive? What new needs do clients have that the network does not cover? For example, if drought has increased demand for fodder and water advice, you may need new contacts in water services and fodder banks.

Adding new role players

New entrants appear all the time: a new abattoir opens, a bank launches an agricultural loan product, a digital platform starts offering weather alerts. Scan local media, attend district forums and ask farmers who they deal with. Introduce new partners to the network with a clear purpose.

Handling problems

When a partner fails to deliver, for example a promised input delivery is late before planting, address it quickly and politely, record the issue, and inform affected farmers honestly. If a partner repeatedly fails or acts unethically, discuss with your supervisor and reduce your reliance on them.

Key points

  • Extension delivery depends on a network of government, research, private and community partners.
  • Map stakeholders by value and interest, starting from client needs.
  • Agree roles clearly and stay within your mandate.
  • Keep a secure, updated contact register and review it regularly.
  • Stay neutral and ethical when recommending partners to farmers.
